Portraits.default_lens_advice: Use 50mm, 85mm, or 70-200mm equivalents. Choose 85mm or 70-200mm for flattering compression and clean backgrounds.
composition: Place the eyes on the upper third and leave looking room in the direction of gaze.
Use distance between subject and background to increase separation.
Shoot near open shade or window light; avoid harsh midday top light.
techniques: Use Eye AF / subject detection if available.
Start around f/1.8-f/2.8 for separation, stopping down for groups.
Use flash or reflector only if it improves catchlights and does not break venue rules.

Wildlife / Birds.default_lens_advice: Use the longest reliable autofocus lens available. 400-600mm is usually the practical range for birds and distant wildlife.
composition: Keep space in the frame in the direction the animal is moving or looking.
Get low where safe to bring the subject closer to eye level.
Look for clean backgrounds before the action starts.
techniques: Use continuous AF, animal/bird detection, and burst shooting.
Start at 1/1000s for perched birds and 1/2000s+ for flight.
Use Auto ISO with a shutter-speed floor rather than letting shutter speed drop too low.

Sports / Action.default_lens_advice: Use 70-200mm for sideline or indoor sports; add longer reach for field sports or motorsport.
composition: Frame slightly loose to allow for unpredictable movement.
Shoot from a position where backgrounds are clean and action comes toward you.
Capture peak gesture, ball contact, landing, celebration, or reaction.
techniques: Use continuous AF with tracking and high-speed burst.
Start at 1/1000s; go 1/2000s+ for fast motorsport or birds-in-flight-like action.
Pre-focus on zones where action repeats.

Landscape.default_lens_advice: Use a wide zoom for foreground-led compositions, a standard zoom for flexibility, and telephoto only for compressed distant details.
composition: Use foreground, midground, and background layers.
Watch horizon placement; avoid splitting the image in half unless symmetry is the point.
Use leading lines, weather, and side light to add depth.
techniques: Use a tripod for blue hour, sunrise, sunset, or focus stacking.
Use CPL for reflections and foliage, but avoid uneven skies on ultra-wide lenses.
Bracket exposures when sky-to-land contrast is high.

Architecture / Interiors.default_lens_advice: Use an ultra-wide lens for tight interiors and a standard zoom for detail frames. Keep the camera level to reduce converging verticals.
composition: Keep verticals straight unless you deliberately want drama.
Use symmetry, doorways, frames, and repeating patterns.
Move the camera position before zooming; small shifts change perspective strongly indoors.
techniques: Use tripod and low ISO when permitted.
Bracket exposures for windows and bright fixtures.
Check edge distortion and avoid placing people at the extreme corners on ultra-wide lenses.

Street / Travel.default_lens_advice: Use a flexible standard zoom or a 35mm equivalent prime for a light, responsive walk-around kit.
composition: Build frames around gestures, layers, reflections, signs, and light pockets.
Keep backgrounds intentional; wait for the right subject to enter the frame.
Use scale: include people, vehicles, or buildings to communicate place.
techniques: Use aperture priority with a minimum shutter speed.
Pre-set exposure compensation for backlight or bright streets.
Carry less so you can move and react quickly.

Events / Stage.default_lens_advice: Use 24-70mm for context and groups, 70-200mm for stage/speeches/candid reactions, and a fast 35mm or 50mm if light is very low.
composition: Mix establishing shots, medium moments, reactions, and tight details.
Shoot from the edges to avoid blocking guests.
Use negative space for signage, screens, or environmental context.
techniques: Check flash rules before using flash.
Use silent or electronic shutter only if banding is not a problem under LED light.
Use Auto ISO and maintain shutter speed high enough for gestures and speaker movement.

Macro / Details.default_lens_advice: Use a true macro lens around 90-105mm for working distance and controllable backgrounds.
composition: Fill the frame with shape, texture, repetition, or one clear detail.
Align the sensor plane with the subject plane when you need more of the subject sharp.
Simplify the background; tiny distractions become large at macro distances.
techniques: Use flash, diffuser, or reflector to control tiny shadows.
Stop down more than usual, but watch diffraction.
Use tripod, focus stacking, or burst shooting when wind is present.

Astrophotography.default_lens_advice: For landscape astro use a fast ultra-wide lens. For deep-sky use a telescope/mount workflow instead of normal handheld/event gear.
composition: Scout foreground before dark and avoid unsafe movement at night.
Use the Milky Way, moon phase, and foreground shapes to anchor the frame.
Keep artificial lights out of the frame unless they are intentional.
techniques: Use manual focus with magnified live view on a bright star.
Start with 10-15s on ultra-wide full-frame lenses, then adjust after checking star trailing.
Use intervalometer and red headlamp; add dew control for longer sessions.

Product / Food.default_lens_advice: Use 50mm/85mm for natural perspective and 100mm macro for small details, jewellery, textures, and food closeups.
composition: Control the background, props, and edge clutter before adjusting camera settings.
Use diagonals, repetition, and negative space for commercial-looking frames.
Keep labels readable and hero details sharp.
techniques: Use soft side light and flags/reflectors to shape highlights.
Use tripod for repeatable framing.
Stop down enough for the product depth; use focus stacking for small objects.
